title: Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% Of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute.
summary: Proposition 44 requires California's nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs) and FQHC "look-alikes" to spend at least 90 percent of their annual revenue on activities that advance their charitable mission, with the state Attorney General defining exactly which expenses count. Clinics that fall short pay a penalty equal to the shortfall into a state-held account, face possible patient lawsuits for breach of charitable trust, and their officers face criminal liability for gaming the calculation. The measure is sponsored and almost entirely funded by the health workers' union SEIU-UHW; it is opposed by the clinics themselves, most major medical and hospital associations, and the state Democratic Party.
what_it_really_means: The measure's own text, titled the "Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act," applies only to Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs) and FQHC "look-alikes" as those terms are defined under federal Medicaid law (42 U.S.C. Section 1396d), roughly 2,000 nonprofit and public safety-net clinics that serve low-income and uninsured Californians. Tribal, tribal-organization, and urban Indian health programs are explicitly excluded. It does not touch for-profit urgent care chains, hospitals, or county-run clinics that aren't structured as FQHCs; the LAO notes most of California's roughly 2,000 safety-net clinics are private nonprofits, with the rest run by counties.

The core mechanic is a new metric the statute calls the "Mission Spend Ratio": total spending on activities that accomplish the clinic's exempt purpose, divided by total revenue. The bill doesn't invent this number from scratch. It anchors it to two lines every nonprofit already reports on IRS Form 990: "total program service expenses" (Part III, line 4e) as the numerator, and "total revenue" (Part I, line 12) as the denominator, using each clinic's 2024 tax-year filing as the baseline. Clinics currently report spending an average of about 80 percent of revenue this way, per the LAO, with wide variation clinic to clinic, so most affected clinics start below the new 90 percent floor on day one.

The statute does not itself define what counts as a "program service" expense beyond that IRS baseline. It hands that power entirely to the state Attorney General, who is authorized to issue "binding guidance" adjusting both figures, including rules for how to treat transactions with a "related party." The text explicitly flags the loophole this guidance is meant to close: a clinic could route money through a related organization, such as a management company, real estate landlord, parent or holding company, staffing company, or "sister" entity (the statute uses the federal Medicare related-party definition at 42 C.F.R. 413.17(b)), in a way that either artificially inflates its program-service spending or artificially shrinks its reported revenue. Whether rent paid to a clinic-affiliated landlord, a "care coordination" contract with a related foundation, or a staffing arrangement with a sister nonprofit counts toward the 90 percent is not settled by the initiative text; it is left to Attorney General guidance issued after the fact, which the Attorney General may adopt by bulletin or notice without going through the state's normal rulemaking process (the measure exempts this guidance from the Administrative Procedure Act's usual notice-and-comment requirements).

Opponents, including the California Primary Care Association and physicians quoted in the official ballot arguments, argue the ambiguity cuts the other way for ordinary clinic operations: capital projects, equipment and technology upgrades, disaster preparedness spending, and operating reserves are, in their reading, at risk of being treated as "non-program" overhead subject to the 10 percent cap, alongside services like patient transportation, health-enrollment navigators, and community health worker programs that clinics count as core to their mission but that a stricter Attorney General definition might not. A study commissioned by the California Primary Care Association, cited in CalMatters' coverage, estimated 91 percent of health centers statewide don't currently meet a 90 percent threshold and could collectively face as much as $1.7 billion in penalties in the first year.

The penalty structure is a clawback-with-parole design, not a flat fine. Each year, the state Department of Public Health assesses a penalty equal to the exact dollar shortfall between a clinic's actual mission-directed spending and 90 percent of its revenue. That money goes into a new Mission Spend Ratio Penalty Account inside the state's Special Deposit Fund, where it sits in escrow for five years. If the clinic comes into compliance with the 90 percent ratio and submits a state-approved plan to spend the money on mission-directed expenses, it gets the money back (minus the state's administrative costs). If a clinic never gets back into compliance within five years, the state keeps the money permanently and the Legislature is authorized to spend it on clinical workforce training, recruitment, and retention programs. In effect, the penalty works as a forced loan to the state that converts to a permanent seizure only after a five-year grace period.

A clinic can ask the Department of Public Health for a one-year waiver of the 90 percent requirement, renewable, based on either "unexpected or exceptional circumstances" or a showing that compliance would threaten the clinic as a "going concern." The statute lists factors like likely facility or program closures, job losses, rural or frontier service areas, and financial distress. But the statute states the waiver decision is "solely and exclusively" within the Department's discretion, with no independent appeal route specified for a denied waiver (as opposed to a disputed penalty calculation, which does get a formal hearing).

Two enforcement mechanisms go beyond the licensing-and-fine model voters might expect from a ballot title about spending ratios. First, Section 5142.1 of the Corporations Code, added by this measure, lets any patient of a non-compliant FQHC sue the clinic directly for breach of charitable trust, a legal claim historically reserved to the Attorney General under existing nonprofit law, and specifies that neither good-faith conduct nor the business-judgment rule, the standard legal shields for nonprofit board decisions, is a defense to that suit. Second, the measure creates a new crime: any clinic director, officer, or agent who knowingly misreports the spending figures, or knowingly routes money through a related party with intent to artificially inflate the Mission Spend Ratio, is subject to a felony punishable under the state's realignment law or up to a year in county jail.

The measure includes a standard same-ballot "competing measure" clause (Section 10): if another measure governing FQHC mission-spend ratios appears on the same ballot, whichever gets more yes votes prevails in its entirety. SEIU-UHW separately qualified a companion measure (Initiative #25-0009) capping healthcare executive compensation at $450,000, but that measure did not make the final 14-measure qualified slate for the November 2026 ballot, so Section 10 has no counterpart to trigger against this year.

The new requirements don't take effect immediately: they apply starting with each clinic's first full fiscal year beginning at least six months after the measure passes, meaning most affected clinics would first be on the hook for fiscal year 2027. Before the vote, the California Primary Care Association and Open Door Community Health Centers sued in federal court (N.D. Cal.) to keep the measure off the ballot, arguing it conflicts with federal law governing FQHC spending; that suit did not succeed in blocking the election.

fiscal_impact.state_cost: Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year for the Attorney General and Department of Public Health to collect data, calculate Mission Spend Ratios, and enforce and adjudicate penalties, per the Legislative Analyst's Office.
fiscal_impact.local_cost: none identified by the LAO as a distinct category; effects on county-run clinics would flow through the same mechanism as other affected clinics if they meet the FQHC definition.
fiscal_impact.revenue_change: None from new taxes; the measure creates no tax. It does create a new state-administered fund (the Mission Spend Ratio Penalty Account) that receives clinic penalty payments, which are escrowed for five years and either refunded to clinics or, if unclaimed, appropriated by the Legislature for clinic workforce programs.
fiscal_impact.ongoing_vs_one_time: Ongoing. Enforcement costs, penalty assessments, and the annual reporting cycle recur every year the law is in effect, beginning with each clinic's first full fiscal year at least six months after passage.
fiscal_impact.narrative: The LAO states state enforcement costs would be in the low tens of millions of dollars annually, intended to be covered by new fees the measure requires the Attorney General to charge affected clinics rather than by the General Fund. Beyond that enforcement cost, the LAO calls the broader fiscal picture uncertain, because it depends on two unknowns: how the Attorney General ultimately defines which expenses count as program services, and how clinics respond. The LAO flags a specific mechanism worth noting: if clinics increase direct health care spending to hit 90 percent, some of that additional spending would serve Medi-Cal patients, which could increase state Medi-Cal costs. Conversely, the LAO notes some clinics that cannot meet the minimum might close instead, which would have its own uncertain fiscal and access effects on state and local governments. Neither the potential $1.7 billion first-year penalty exposure cited by the opposition-funded California Primary Care Association study, nor any estimate of how many clinics would actually pay penalties versus adjust their spending, appears in the LAO's own analysis. The LAO's number reflects only the state's administrative and enforcement cost, not the total penalties clinics might pay, which functionally circulate within the fund rather than being a net cost or revenue to government unless never reimbursed.

new_spending_areas: California Attorney General's Office: new staffing to collect clinic financial data, calculate Mission Spend Ratios annually, issue binding guidance on qualifying expenses, and conduct audits
California Department of Public Health: new staffing to assess and collect penalties, adjudicate disputes and waiver requests, and administer the Mission Spend Ratio Penalty Account

Mission Spend Ratio Penalty Account (within the state Special Deposit Fund): holds clinic penalty payments in five-year escrow; money unclaimed after five years may be appropriated by the Legislature for clinical worker training, recruitment, and retention programs
spending.funding_source: A new mandatory annual registration fee charged to affected clinics, set by the Attorney General in consultation with the Department of Public Health to cover the state's administrative and enforcement costs; the measure directs that fees, not the General Fund, pay for implementation.

control_and_power: The California Attorney General gains sole authority to issue binding guidance defining which clinic expenses count toward the 90 percent "program services" threshold, including how to treat transactions with related organizations such as affiliated landlords, management companies, or staffing entities, and may do so by bulletin or notice without the standard Administrative Procedure Act rulemaking process. The Attorney General also calculates each clinic's Mission Spend Ratio annually and may audit clinics and their contractors or related parties. The Department of Public Health gains authority to assess penalties, grant or deny one-year compliance waivers at its "sole and exclusive" discretion, and decide whether a clinic's five-years-escrowed penalty money is returned. The measure also transfers a form of enforcement power to private individuals: any patient of a non-compliant clinic may sue that clinic for breach of charitable trust, a claim ordinarily reserved to the Attorney General under existing nonprofit law, and the clinic's board cannot raise good-faith conduct or the business-judgment rule as a defense. That removes protections nonprofit directors otherwise have when a court reviews their spending decisions.
loopholes: The statute sets the 90 percent numerical threshold but does not itself define which expenses qualify as "program services" beyond a 2024 IRS Form 990 baseline; that substantive line-drawing is delegated entirely to after-the-fact Attorney General guidance, so what actually counts toward compliance is not fixed by the text voters are approving and could change from year to year at the Attorney General's discretion.

The related-party definition (borrowed from federal Medicare rules at 42 C.F.R. 413.17(b)) covers management companies, landlords, parent/holding companies, staffing entities, and "sister" organizations, and the statute's own findings acknowledge these relationships could be used to artificially inflate program-service spending or shrink reported revenue. The statute directs the Attorney General to address this in guidance but does not itself close the gap, leaving a transition window between the law's passage and the issuance of that guidance during which the related-party rules are undefined.

The Department of Public Health's waiver process is described as "solely and exclusively" within its discretion, with detailed factors for the clinic to document but no explicit standard of review or appeal path if a waiver is denied, unlike the formal hearing process available to a clinic that disputes its Mission Spend Ratio calculation or penalty amount.

Because the reporting baseline is drawn from each clinic's own 2024 IRS Form 990, and the Attorney General is authorized to "adjust" both the numerator and denominator based on guidance issued after the fact, the practical spending floor a given clinic must hit is not fully knowable at the time voters cast a ballot on the measure.

The measure exempts the Attorney General's guidance-issuing process under this section from the Administrative Procedure Act's normal rulemaking requirements (notice, comment, formal adoption), and separately states that Health and Safety Code Section 1229.1 does not apply to violations based on standards adopted this way. Both changes reduce the normal procedural and appeal safeguards that would otherwise apply to a new binding regulatory standard of this kind.
unexpected_provisions: Section 5142.1 of the Corporations Code, added by this measure, lets any patient of a non-compliant clinic sue that clinic for breach of charitable trust, a cause of action normally brought only by the state Attorney General, and explicitly bars the clinic from raising good-faith conduct or the business-judgment rule as a defense, which are the standard legal protections nonprofit board members rely on when their spending and operating decisions are challenged in court. Nothing in the ballot title or summary flags this new avenue for private lawsuits against clinics.

The measure creates a new criminal offense: a clinic director, officer, or agent who knowingly misreports the spending or revenue figures, or knowingly routes funds through a related party intending to artificially inflate the Mission Spend Ratio, faces a felony under the state's realignment sentencing law or up to a year in county jail. A ballot title about a spending percentage does not suggest new individual criminal liability for clinic executives.

The measure's official statutory title, the "Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act," is broader-sounding than the narrower ballot title about a 90 percent spending requirement that voters will actually see.

The Attorney General's guidance-writing power under this measure is explicitly exempted from the state's standard administrative rulemaking process (the Administrative Procedure Act's notice-and-comment requirements), letting a single statewide official set binding financial-reporting standards for an entire sector by bulletin rather than through the public rulemaking process that would normally apply to a rule of this consequence.

The measure includes a standard same-ballot competing-measure clause (Section 10) that would have nullified a companion SEIU-UHW measure capping healthcare executive pay at $450,000 had that measure also qualified for the ballot; it did not make the final 14-measure slate, so the clause is dormant for this election but signals the sponsor's broader campaign against clinic executive compensation and overhead.
pros: Vote YES on Prop. 44 to put patients first: supporters argue the measure mandates that community health clinics spend at least 90 percent of revenue on patient care and services, with new transparency and accountability requirements that don't currently exist in state law.

Brisa Barrera, a healthcare worker at a Santa Rosa community clinic, argues clinics receive public dollars to serve vulnerable populations, and when that money is "siphoned off for bloated administrative costs, it's the patients and workers who suffer," so the measure directs resources to clinics and care rather than overhead.

SEIU-UHW spokesperson Renée Saldaña argues the mission-spend definition is broader than critics claim: it covers all the ancillary services a clinic provides in addition to direct patient care, not narrowly defined "patient care" spending alone, so legitimate wraparound services are not automatically excluded.

Supporters point to findings in the measure's own text that some clinics report annual surpluses as high as 20 percent of revenue and management/administrative costs as high as 30 to 40 percent of revenue at the highest-spending clinics, arguing a spending floor is a reasonable response to that documented variation.

The measure directs unclaimed penalty money after five years toward clinical worker training, recruitment, and retention, which supporters frame as directly addressing chronic understaffing, high workloads, and turnover that clinic workers report, as cited in the measure's findings.
cons: Opponents led by the California Medical Association, California Academy of Family Physicians, and American Academy of Pediatrics California argue the measure would cut roughly $1.7 billion from clinics in its first year alone based on a California Primary Care Association-commissioned study, forcing an estimated 88 to 91 percent of clinics to operate at a loss or face steep penalties.

Graciela Soto, CEO of Altura Community Clinic in Tulare, argues services her clinic already provides, such as free patient transportation and community health screenings and education for farmworkers, might not count as "mission service" under a stricter Attorney General definition and would be at risk of being cut.

Dr. Brent Sugimoto of the California Academy of Family Physicians warns the measure penalizes clinics for spending on capital projects, new equipment and technology upgrades, disaster preparedness, and financial reserves, which are investments clinics need to keep operating safely and through emergencies.

Jodi Hicks, CEO of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, argues the measure risks forcing clinics to close at a time when patients already face reduced access due to federal healthcare funding cuts, calling the timing especially damaging.

The rebuttal to the argument in favor, signed by physician leaders including the presidents of the California Academy of Family Physicians and American College of Emergency Physicians' California chapter, states the measure is "written and funded entirely by one special interest" and argues existing state and federal oversight of clinic spending is already adequate.

Carmela Coyle, president and CEO of the California Hospital Association, argues the measure arrives at an especially precarious time for health care funding and will make it difficult or impossible for clinics to recruit and retain the mission-driven leadership needed to preserve access to care.

Opponents argue the measure hands an elected Attorney General with no healthcare background effective control over which clinic services count toward mission spending, inserting a political official into clinical operating decisions that clinic boards and management are normally responsible for.

nonpartisan_analysis.summary: The LAO describes Proposition 44 as requiring private nonprofit safety-net clinics to spend at least 90 percent of total annual revenue on health care services, with the Attorney General defining in more detail which expenses count using existing federal reports as a starting point, and clinics able to request temporary waivers. It notes clinics currently report spending an average of about 80 percent of revenue on health care services, with variation across clinics. Non-compliant clinics must pay a penalty equal to the shortfall, refundable within five years if they come into compliance, otherwise retained by the state for clinic workforce programs. The LAO estimates state enforcement costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered by fees on affected clinics, and flags other costs as uncertain, depending on how the Attorney General defines qualifying expenses and how clinics respond, including possible increased Medi-Cal costs if clinics shift more spending to direct patient services, or uncertain effects if clinics close rather than comply.

Provides the full official measure design, campaign finance data, and background. It documents the initiative's official text as the "Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act," details the Mission Spend Ratio calculation and its tie to IRS Form 990 reporting categories, and describes the penalty, waiver, appeal, and criminal-penalty provisions in full. It reports the measure was sponsored by Californians for Responsible Healthcare (SEIU-UHW West), qualified for the ballot on May 18, 2026 with 634,061 valid signatures of 1,030,848 submitted, and is opposed by the California Hospital Association, California Primary Care Association, and Open Door Community Health Centers, the latter two having sued (unsuccessfully, as of this measure's qualification) in federal court to keep it off the ballot. A Public Policy Institute of California poll from September 2026 found 34% support and 61% opposition among likely voters.

Summarizes the measure as requiring nonprofit safety-net clinics to spend at least 90% of revenue on patient care, with the state attorney general issuing guidance on qualifying expenses and the state empowered to fine noncompliant clinics. It identifies SEIU-UHW as the sponsor, following a failed legislative attempt the prior year, and notes opposition from the California Primary Care Association, California Medical Association, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, California Hospital Association, and the California Democratic Party, who warn of clinic closures and cite a $1.7 billion first-year penalty exposure estimate from a CPCA-commissioned study.
